title: It was found that in 32% of AI usage cases, using a cheaper model resulted in higher overall costs.
source_used: GIGAZINE (English edition), 6 Oct 2026, read from fulltext/C01-04.txt (HTTP 200); the paper's arXiv page (2603.23971) checked once for its dates and abstract
key_facts: A research team from Stanford University, Carnegie Mellon University, UC Berkeley and Microsoft Research had eight state-of-the-art AI models do over 6,800 tasks, including math, programming and science, to compare low-cost and high-cost models.
In 32% of cases the low-cost model ended up costing more overall.

Example: asked to analyse a YouTube video frame by frame, the high-priced Gemini 3.1 Pro finished in 85 steps for $1; the low-priced Gemini 3 Flash took over 1,000 steps, failed to complete the task and cost $14.
The team blames the AI's 'overthinking' and 'over-acting': complex tasks need more reasoning steps and actions, so a stronger model can sometimes run a task faster and cheaper.
In another test Gemini 3 Flash used more than 60,000 thinking tokens where GPT-5.4 solved the problem with only 25 tokens.
Repeating the same instructions on the same model, the most expensive trial cost 9.7 times the cheapest.
Lead author 'Lin Zhao Chen' is quoted as saying you should not judge which model is cheap based solely on price.
The study is named as 'The Price Reversal Phenomenon: When Cheaper Reasoning Models Cost More' (PDF 2603.23971v2).
quote_evidence: The results showed that in 32% of cases, the low-cost model ended up costing more overall.
The research team points out that the cause is the AI's 'overthinking' and 'over-acting.'
The cost of the task was $1 (approximately 158 yen) for the former and $14 (approximately 2211 yen) for the latter.
why_it_matters_hint: A lower listed price does not guarantee a lower bill: cheaper models can think and act far longer on hard tasks, so cost has to be judged per task.
event_date: Study first posted 25 Mar 2026 (v1) and last revised 28 May 2026 (v2), per its arXiv page checked on 6 Oct 2026; GIGAZINE's write-up is dated 6 Oct 2026 (02:36 UTC).
notes: OLDER NEWS RE-DATED: the arXiv record (arxiv.org/abs/2603.23971, authors Lingjiao Chen, Chi Zhang, Yeye He, Ion Stoica, Matei Zaharia, James Zou; no comments or journal reference shown) says submitted 25 Mar 2026, last revised 28 May 2026; GIGAZINE's write-up adds no new research, so freshness is FOLLOW-UP of 28 May 2026 and the item is a held-back candidate for qa_check. GIGAZINE's 'Lin Zhao Chen' appears to be first author Lingjiao Chen. Differences between GIGAZINE and the abstract: the abstract says 32% of model-pair comparisons (GIGAZINE says 32% of cases) and 12 task sets (GIGAZINE says over 6,800 tasks); the 9.7x figure is thinking-token variation in the abstract but cost in GIGAZINE, so the summary uses 'comparisons', 'thousands of tasks' and leaves the 9.7x figure out. The tested models (GPT-5.4, Gemini 3 Flash and 3.1 Pro) predate the paper's May revision. Preprint, no outside review reported.
